The instruction is simple: write whatever comes. But the moment I sit down to obey, the mind becomes a crowd of possibilities. There is a strange pressure in the blank page. It is not exactly fear of judgment—no one is grading this, no one is waiting with a red pen. It is more like standing at a crossroads with a thousand roads, and each road is a sentence, and each sentence leads to a different landscape. Choose the wrong one and the whole journey changes. Choose the right one and you might still never know what the others held. So you sit, and you hesitate, and then you write something just to move, because motion is better than stillness, and the first word is the hardest.

What comes to me now is the memory of a window in my childhood bedroom. The glass was old and slightly wavy, and when I pressed my face against it, the world outside looked soft, as if I were seeing it through water. There was a maple tree in the yard, and in autumn its leaves turned the color of rust and honey. I used to believe that tree was the oldest thing in existence. It was only a few decades old, but to a child, anything taller than your father is ancient. I would sit on the floor with a book in my lap and glance at the tree between paragraphs. Its branches moved in the wind, not all together but one at a time, like a person thinking through a decision. I loved that tree without understanding why. It was simply there, quiet and constant, and it did not ask anything of me.

Eventually we moved. The tree stayed, of course. Trees stay. People leave. That is one of the truths you learn early, though it takes a long time to feel it in your bones. I sometimes wonder if the tree still stands. I could look it up on a map, I suppose, but I don't want to know. Knowing would end the question, and the question is more alive than the answer. The maple in my mind is always October, always full of light, always dropping a few leaves onto the grass as if offering them to the ground. I have written many things in my life, but I have never managed to describe that tree in a way that satisfies me. The words are always too heavy or too light. They miss the texture of the bark, the particular green of the leaves against a blue sky, the way the shadows moved across my bedroom wall in the afternoon.

This is the trouble with memory. It is not a photograph; it is a painting that repaints itself every time you look at it. The details shift. The colors deepen. And yet I trust it more than I trust the present moment. The present is always slipping away, always becoming something else. But memory, at least, is mine. I can hold it in my mind like a smooth stone worn down by the river of years. I can turn it over and over and find new edges, new glints, new places where the light catches unexpectedly.

I think that is why I write. Not to record, but to hold. To take the fleeting things—a tree, a voice, a laugh, the smell of rain on warm asphalt—and give them a place to live. Words are fragile containers. They leak. They are never quite waterproof. But they are all we have when the thing itself is gone. We write eulogies for people we loved and places we lost. We write letters to the future. We write reminders to ourselves that we were here, that we saw this, that we felt this strange and crushing and beautiful thing called being alive.

Lately I have been thinking about language itself. There are so many words, and yet there are no words for some of the most important moments. That moment just after someone leaves the room, when you still feel their presence like a warmth in the chair. The feeling of waking from a dream and knowing it was important but not knowing why. The ache that comes from a song you haven't heard in years, a song that suddenly brings back an entire afternoon you had forgotten you lived. There are German words for some of these feelings, or at least attempts—Fernweh, the longing for distant places; Waldeinsamkeit, the feeling of being alone in the woods; Torschlusspanik, the fear of doors closing. But most of our inner lives remain unlabeled, wild, unnamed. We stumble through them with approximations and metaphors, trying to say what cannot be said.

And maybe that is okay. Maybe the unsayable is exactly what keeps us writing. If everything could be put into words, we would stop speaking. We would become quiet. But we are not quiet. We whisper, we shout, we write in journals and on napkins, we press send on texts at three in the morning. We are creatures of speech, but not because speech is perfect. We speak because we are full, and fullness wants to spill. We speak because silence is too heavy to carry alone. We speak because there is another person somewhere who might hear us, and hearing, know they are not alone either.

I think of the people I have loved. They drift through my mind like leaves on a river. Some are still in my life, some are gone, some are simply no longer part of the story, though they once seemed essential. It is strange how time does that. It rearranges the furniture of our lives without asking permission. You wake up one day and realize that the person who meant everything to you no longer even crosses your mind unless a certain smell or song calls them back. And that is not betrayal. That is healing. That is the heart making room for new things, new mornings, new sorrows and joys.

What will I write tomorrow? I have no idea. That is the wonderful and terrifying thing about a blank page. It is always waiting. It does not judge. It does not care if today's words are clumsy or wise. It simply offers its empty field, and you walk across it, leaving footprints of ink. Some days those footprints lead somewhere. Some days they are just footprints, shapes without meaning. But even then, the walking is worthwhile.

The sun is going down now. I can see it from the window, a low orange disc sinking behind the rooftops. The light in the room has turned golden and soft. I think of the maple tree again, and I wonder if it is still standing. I hope it is. I hope someone is sitting under it, a child with a book, glancing up between paragraphs, watching the branches move one at a time, like a person thinking through a decision. I hope they will remember it for the rest of their life. I hope they will not need to look it up on a map. I hope they will just let the question live.

A thousand words is not enough to say all of this. It is barely enough to begin. But it is enough to remind me that the world is full of things worth noticing, and that noticing is a kind of prayer. The words will never be perfect. The tree will never be fully described. But the attempt matters. It always matters. So here I am, writing whatever comes. And what comes is gratitude—for the blank page, for the light, for the memory of a tree, for you, reading these words, for the strange and miraculous fact that we can reach across time and space with nothing but marks on a screen. That, too, is a kind of tree, growing in the forest of human connection. Let us keep planting. Let us keep writing.
